findings.title: Denial of service via unbounded byte array allocation
findings.impact: A remote attacker can craft an AMQP frame with a large contentLength value to consume all available heap memory, causing the Java process to crash or become unresponsive. This is a direct denial of service attack.
findings.evidence: Lines 86-90: The method reads a 32-bit unsigned integer from the network and uses it to allocate a byte array. The code `if(contentLength < Integer.MAX_VALUE)` allows allocation of up to Integer.MAX_VALUE - 1 bytes (approximately 2 GB). An attacker sending a frame with contentLength near 2 GB will exhaust available heap memory, causing OutOfMemoryError and denial of service.

findings.title: Potential integer overflow in timestamp conversion
findings.impact: A malformed AMQP frame with a timestamp value close to Long.MAX_VALUE will cause silent integer overflow, resulting in a Date object with an incorrect (negative) timestamp. This could cause unexpected behavior in code relying on timestamp ordering or comparisons.
findings.evidence: Line 269: `return new Date(in.readLong()*1000);` multiplies an untrusted network-supplied long value by 1000 without overflow checking. If the input long value is close to Long.MAX_VALUE/1000 (approximately 9.22e15), the multiplication will overflow and produce a negative date.

defects_to_look_for.mechanism: A length field read from untrusted input decides the size of a buffer, and that buffer is created before the corresponding payload has been shown to exist.
Decoding routines call one another in a cycle with nothing counting how deep the cycle has gone, so nesting in the input controls the depth.
